name: Iron-Maw Singularity

detectability.signature: Deep gravimetric well with no emission source; background starlight smears into a thin accretion-bright ring visible on long-range optics

proximity: Navigation solutions drift up to 40,000 km off course unless continuously corrected
Long-range sensors return doubled and mirrored images of everything beyond the horizon
contact: Crossing the photon sphere shreds hulls along the tidal stress axis
All telemetry ceases; nothing transmitted past the horizon ever returns
prolonged_exposure: Orbit decay becomes unrecoverable within six hours of entering the capture band
Time dilation desynchronizes crew biometrics from shipboard clocks by months to years

phenomena: Time dilation effects near the boundary
known_incidents: The freighter Kassiope's Lament was lost with all hands after total engine failure at 900 km
Meridian Survey Station 12 holds a permanent observation orbit at a cautious 2 million km
description: From a distance the Iron-Maw Singularity announces itself only by absence: a perfect black disc ringed by a hair-thin arc of crushed starlight. Long-range gravimetrics show a well so steep that sensor pings bend visibly around it, doubling every image taken through the field. At thirty-eight kilometers across, the horizon itself is small, but its influence dominates the entire sector.

The singularity never moves and never varies, which is the only mercy it offers. Approach trajectories can be computed to the meter, yet any drift into the capture band ends in irreversible spiral decay. Ships lingering near the boundary report clocks sliding out of agreement with fleet standard time, and hull welds creak under tidal gradients that strengthen by the kilometer.

Charted four centuries ago after the loss of Kassiope's Lament, the Iron-Maw has since become the sector's most studied gravitational object. Its clean, isolated mass makes it an ideal natural laboratory for testing relativity under extreme conditions. Research stations maintain distant orbits, and salvage firms quietly mark its capture band as the richest wreck repository in the region.

Today the anomaly remains a fixed landmark and a standing warning on every commercial route plot. Physicists lease observation time aboard Station 12, while military planners note that nothing hostile can approach unseen through its lensing glare. Travelers who respect the two-million-kilometer line have nothing to fear; those who cross it become data points.
